Real ballot, researched with this tool on October 16, 2026 using a public building's address. AI research can be wrong: open the sources. This is not an endorsement. Get dates and places from your official election office (San Francisco Department of Elections (also California Secretary of State)).

Address used: San Francisco City Hall (public building).

The tool is neutral by default; the profile table shows how values match works.

Method

Each choice is shown side by side, with no scores. Records (what candidates did) come first, then questionnaire answers, then other statements, then donors and endorsements. Every line shows its kind, topic, date and source. After each comparison, a table shows how six example values profiles would score it from the same evidence; those scores are illustrations, not recommendations.

U.S. Representative, District 11

Two candidates, both printed as Democratic, are on the general ballot for the seat held by Nancy Pelosi, who is not on the ballot.

Connie Chan

  • [Housing] RECORD, 2025-11-20: Reported (Mission Local, Nov 20, 2025; date of the act not given): as District 1 Supervisor she attempted to pass amendments to "exempt existing housing stock" from the mayor's upzoning plan. Per the article, the amendments were not integrated because they "would have effectively gutted it and made it noncompliant with state requirements." (source: missionlocal.org)
  • [Great Highway] RECORD, 2026-09: Per Mission Local, in January 2026 she was the first to sign a failed measure to reopen the Great Highway, and she backs Prop G. (source: missionlocal.org)
  • [Great Highway] STATED, 2025-11: Mission Local reports she opposed Proposition K (2024, removing cars from the Great Highway). (source: missionlocal.org)
  • [AI and labor] STATED, 2026-10-13: At the Oct 13 forum she proposed taxing companies that use automation so they lack an incentive to replace workers, and said Wiener weakened SB 53 working with industry (Mission Local recap). (source: missionlocal.org)
  • [Campaign finance] FUNDER, 2026-06-30: FEC committee page: $1,094,321.06 raised and $732,236.42 spent for 2025-11-20 to 2026-06-30; cash on hand $362,084.64; debts $25,000. Oct quarterly (due Oct 15) not shown or retrievable. (source: www.fec.gov)

Scott Wiener

  • [Housing] RECORD, 2025-10-10: Senator's office page: he authored SB 79 (Abundant and Affordable Homes Near Transit Act), signed Oct 10, 2025; it sets state height standards near major transit stops. Final vote counts differ across sources and were not confirmed on leginfo (blocked), so UNVERIFIED. (source: sd11.senate.ca.gov)
  • [Great Highway] STATED, 2026-09: Per Mission Local, he opposes Prop G, authored the official argument against it in the voter pamphlet, and spoke at the No on G kickoff on Aug 16. (source: missionlocal.org)
  • [AI and housing] STATED, 2026-10-13: At the Oct 13 forum he said he wrote SB 53 and did not weaken it, and blamed high rents on a long failure to build enough housing (Mission Local recap). (source: missionlocal.org)
  • [Campaign finance] FUNDER, 2026-06-30: FEC committee page: $4,561,120.07 raised and $3,326,427.62 spent for 2023-01-01 to 2026-06-30; cash on hand $1,234,692.45; debts $157,266.82. Oct quarterly (due Oct 15) not shown or retrievable. (source: www.fec.gov)
  • [Outside spending] FUNDER, 2026-10-13: SF Standard: Public First Action gave $1M in August and $2M in September, bringing its total to the pro-Wiener Abundant Future PAC to $3.5M (per a spokesperson, not the FEC). Anthropic gave the group $40M, which it says cannot be spent on races; the group has other donors it has not disclosed. Wiener says no Anthropic money is in this race; Chan's campaign disputes that. (source: sfstandard.com)

What to check: How do the candidates' housing and local-transportation records and positions compare, and which matters to you?

State Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers)

Initiative constitutional amendment and statute that would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on net worth over $1 billion for California residents as of Jan 1, 2026.

What YES does:

  • YES: billionaires who were California residents on Jan 1, 2026 would owe a one-time tax of up to 5% of net worth, due in 2027 (payable over five years at extra cost); 90% of revenue for health care, 10% for education or food assistance. https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-title-summ-analysis.pdf

What NO means: NO: no wealth tax is imposed and current tax law is unchanged. https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-title-summ-analysis.pdf

Cost estimate: Legislative Analyst: temporary revenue increase probably in the tens of billions of dollars over several years, very hard to predict; possible ongoing income-tax decrease of less than $1 billion per year; administration costs possibly tens of millions per year. If Prop 41 or 42 gets more yes votes, courts could find a conflict that blocks Prop 40. https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-title-summ-analysis.pdf

Strongest argument for YES: Argument in official guide (as summarized): the tax addresses federal health-care funding cuts. Supporters include SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Ro Khanna and some labor unions (AP, Oct 9); support committees total $32,213,823 through Oct 6, 2026 (Secretary of State). (voterguide.sos.ca.gov)

Strongest argument for NO: Argument in official guide (as summarized): it is a flawed one-time scheme that hurts the economy and does not lower health-care costs. Opponents include California Teachers Association and California Medical Association; opposition committees total $99,596,279 through Oct 6, 2026 (Secretary of State). AP (Oct 9) also lists Gov. Gavin Newsom and Planned Parenthood as opponents. (voterguide.sos.ca.gov)

  • [Taxes] RECORD, 2026: Official Legislative Analyst estimate: tens of billions in temporary revenue; possible ongoing income-tax loss under $1 billion per year. (source: vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov)
  • [Taxes] FUNDER, 2026-10-06: Support committees reported $32,213,823 and opposition committees $99,596,279 through Oct 6, 2026 (Secretary of State); largest support committee YES ON 40 (SEIU-UHW) $31,510,329, largest opposition committee NO ON PROP 40 $88,721,279. (source: www.sos.ca.gov)
  • [Taxes] FUNDER, 2026-10-09: AP (Oct 9): opponents have raised over $300 million, nearly a third from Sergey Brin, with about $96 million in ads spent or booked versus about $209,000 by supporters; the Secretary of State total above is far lower. (source: spectrumnews1.com)

What to check: Whether a one-time wealth tax on billionaires, with 90% of revenue for health care, is worth the uncertain revenue and the possible loss of some ongoing income-tax revenue.

San Francisco Proposition H (Parcel Tax to Fund Muni Operations)

Ordinance that would create a new annual parcel tax from July 1, 2027 through June 30, 2042 to fund Muni service.

What YES does:

  • YES: the City funds Muni service through a new annual parcel tax (2027 base tax $129 single-family, $249 multifamily, $799 non-residential, plus square-footage rates; inflation-adjusted; many seniors discounted or exempt; up to 50% pass-through to rent-controlled tenants capped at $65 per unit per year). https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/Final_Digest_-_Parcel_Tax_to_Fund_Muni_Operations.pdf

What NO means: NO: no parcel tax is created; Muni keeps its current funding sources. https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/Final_Digest_-_Parcel_Tax_to_Fund_Muni_Operations.pdf

Cost estimate: City Controller economic impact report: tax would generate $184 million per year; Controller estimates 800 to 1,445 additional jobs and $310 to $400 million in GDP on average over 15 years versus a scenario with service cuts. This is an economic impact report, separate from the pamphlet Controller's statement below. https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/MUNI_parcel_tax_economic_impact_final.pdf Pamphlet Controller's statement (p. 125): about $177 million per year from FY2027-28, growing with inflation adjustments; administration costs about $2 to $3 million one-time and $4 to $6 million per year. https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/N26_EN_VIP.pdf

Strongest argument for YES: Official proponent argument (Mayor Daniel Lurie and others): Muni is a lifeline for workers, seniors and students; without Prop H service could be cut by 30% and at least 20 bus routes eliminated; the tax funds only Muni service, with oversight and independent audits. (api.sf.gov)

Strongest argument for NO: Official opponent argument (San Francisco Republican Party): the 15-year tax has no binding cost-cutting or efficiency requirements and no results-based sunset; the efficiency review comes in April 2028, after collection starts, and reports only to SFMTA's board; a square-footage tax is flat rather than value-based, and landlords can pass part of it to tenants. (api.sf.gov)

  • [Transit] RECORD, 2026: City Controller report: $184 million annual revenue; 800 to 1,445 jobs and $310 to $400 million GDP over 15 years relative to the cuts scenario. (source: media.api.sf.gov)
  • [Transit] RECORD, 2026-09: Pamphlet Controller's statement on Prop H: about $177 million per year from FY2027-28; administration costs about $2 to $3 million one-time and $4 to $6 million per year. (source: media.api.sf.gov)
  • [Transit] FUNDER, 2026-06-30: Yes committee raised $3.5 million as of end of June, with $500,000 each from OpenAI, Anthropic, Airbnb and Ripple Labs (Mission Local). No opposition committee total was found. (source: missionlocal.org)

What to check: Whether a new parcel tax is the right way to fund Muni operations, compared with possible service cuts and other funding sources.

Open items

  • How contests were chosen: the official SF Voter Information Pamphlet (sfelections.gov/vip, N26_EN_VIP.pdf, created Sept 4, 2026 per the PDF) is citywide and covers all districts. Contests are kept for City Hall's districts: the Census Bureau geocoder (120th Congressional and 2026 State Legislative layers) gives Congressional District 11 and Assembly District 17, and SF open data (data.sf.gov f2zs-jevy) gave Supervisorial District 5, which has no race in 2026 (even-numbered districts only). The pamphlet lists District 11 or 15 and District 17 or 19 by address, so confirm in the SF Voter Portal.
  • Ballot order follows the pamphlet's contest list and Ballot Worksheet (pp. 5, 246-248); the printed card-by-card layout of the personal sample ballot was not seen.
  • Board of Equalization District 2 appears on every SF ballot per the pamphlet. BART District 8: the pamphlet shows only Sara Barz for District 8, but whether this address is in BART District 8 was not confirmed from an official lookup.
  • Board of Education: the pamphlet carries statements for all 8 names, so the earlier 'qualification unverified' note is cleared for the pamphlet; confirm on the personal sample ballot.
  • State Senate District 11 (Scott Wiener) and U.S. Senate: no contest in the pamphlet's contest list for this address; the state senate seat is not on the Nov 2026 SF ballot list.
  • SF measure descriptions rely on pamphlet titles; full pamphlet analyses were read only for the Prop H Controller's statement and arguments. Prop RTM, Props A-G, I, J: text, fiscal statements and ballot arguments not reviewed.
  • No withdrawal found in the pamphlet; the earlier news report of a District 8 supervisorial withdrawal is moot for this address. Write-in candidates (list posted Oct 23 at sfelections.gov/writein) are not covered.
  • Wiener SB 79 final-passage vote counts (event wiener-sb79): UNVERIFIED; leginfo could not be opened and sources disagree.
  • Official SF Voter Information Pamphlet read for the contest list, ballot worksheet, candidate statements list and the Prop H Controller's statement; the personal sample ballot for this address was not seen, and district assignments are from geocoders, not the SF Voter Portal.
  • FEC: the Oct quarterly (through Sept 30, due Oct 15) was not visible on the FEC committee pages or retrievable; CD11 finance rows are through June 30. The OpenFEC API was rate-limited. Outside-spending figures for Abundant Future PAC come from a news report, not the FEC.
  • Wiener SB 79 final-passage votes not confirmed on leginfo (blocked); sources disagree on counts.
  • No Chan board votes with dates and vote counts found; her record rows rely on Mission Local reporting. Oct 13 forum rows rely on the Mission Local recap, not the recording.
  • Governor: no Oct 6-16 debate or new position found; KMPH Oct 6 totals have no period or cash on hand. Cal-Access pre-election reports were not read.
  • Prop H: no opposition funding total found; Ethics Commission filings not read. Official proponent and opponent arguments read from the sf.gov PDFs (scanned; text read by OCR).
  • Prop 40: argument text taken from the official guide page as summarized by the fetch tool; AP's $300 million+ opposition figure conflicts with the Secretary of State totals.
  • Raju appeal: only the April stays were found; the June 30 Daily Journal briefing report is paywalled; no merits ruling found.
  • Public Defender is uncontested, so there is no comparison; Assessor-Recorder and other offices not researched.
  • Community College Board: the pamphlet prints "Lisa Palagi Wynn II" while sf.gov says "Lisa Wynn"; UNVERIFIED which form is the ballot name.
  • CD11: outside spending supporting Chan was not researched; Wiener has said she is backed by outside groups (SF Standard, Oct 13).
